relationship: Thirst and longing for God
rationale: The deer longing for water expresses the soul's longing for God. Psalm62 likewise describes the soul thirsting for God and the flesh longing for Him in a waterless land; the speakers use water deprivation to express desire for God.

relationship: Longing to approach the living God
rationale: The soul thirsts for the living God and asks when it will appear before His face. Psalm83 joins longing for the Lord's courts with heart and flesh exulting in the living God, connecting desire for divine presence with that particular designation.

relationship: Tears as food
rationale: The speaker's tears became bread by day and night. Psalm79 asks whether God will feed the people bread of tears and give them tears to drink; both make prolonged grief into the sufferer's food.

relationship: Approaching God with exultation and thanksgiving
rationale: The speaker remembers and pours out his soul, then says he will pass through the tent to God's house with exultation and thanksgiving. Psalm94 invites people to exult and come before God with thanksgiving; the shared approach to God has those two expressions of praise.

relationship: Mercy and song across day and night
rationale: The psalm anticipates the Lord commanding mercy by day and has His song and prayer at night. Psalm91 commends music to God with declaration of mercy in the morning and truth by night. The daily rhythm joins mercy and worship, with different actions assigned to God and the worshippers.

relationship: Questioning rejection under enemy oppression
rationale: Psalm41 asks God why He has forgotten the speaker and why the speaker goes downcast while an enemy oppresses. Psalm42 repeats the downcast and enemy question after asking why God has thrust him away; the opening descriptions of God's apparent withdrawal differ.

relationship: The reproach asking where God is
rationale: The enemies reproach the speaker with 'Where is your God?' Psalm113 asks that the nations not say 'Where is their God?' Both make denial of God's apparent presence a hostile challenge, without identifying the enemies as the same group.

relationship: Appeal for God to judge a case against wrongdoers
rationale: Psalm42 asks God to judge the speaker's case against an unholy nation and rescue him from an unjust, deceitful person. Psalm34 opens by asking the Lord to judge those who wrong the speaker; both seek divine adjudication against hostile wrongdoers, with Psalm34 also using warfare language.

relationship: The repeated downcast question
rationale: Both speakers question God's apparent withdrawal and ask why they go downcast while an enemy oppresses. Psalm42 says God thrust him away, whereas Psalm41 asks why God forgot him; the repeated question preserves that difference.

relationship: Divine truth as guidance
rationale: Psalm42 asks God to send His light and truth, then says they guided and brought him to His holy mountain and dwellings. Psalm24 asks God to guide the speaker into His truth and teach His paths. Both connect truth with divine guidance, without changing Psalm42's completed guidance into a wholly future action.

relationship: Altar approach joined to praise
rationale: Psalm42 anticipates going to God's altar and giving thanks with a lyre. Psalm25 anticipates going around God's altar to hear praise and recount His wonders. Both place praise at an approach to the altar, while describing different movements and sounds.

relationship: The refrain shared by adjacent laments
rationale: Psalm42 ends with the same questions to the deeply grieved soul, command to hope in God, and anticipated thanksgiving found in Psalm41. The repeated wording makes a concrete literary connection between the neighboring poems.

relationship: Fathers transmitting God's ancient works
rationale: The community says its fathers announced the work God did in ancient days. Psalm77 likewise speaks of what the fathers recounted and of announcing the Lord's mighty acts and wonders to another generation; both explicitly transmit divine deeds through generations.

relationship: God planting His people
rationale: Psalm43 contrasts God's destruction of nations with His planting of the fathers. The sea song asks God to bring and plant His people in the mountain of His inheritance. The planting image describes divine establishment of the people, expressed as remembered action and petition respectively.

relationship: God as King who brings salvation
rationale: Psalm43 calls God its King and asks Him to command Jacob's salvations. Psalm73 calls God the community's King and says He worked salvation in the earth. The particular pairing of divine kingship and salvation appears as petition and retrospective confession.

relationship: Rejection and God's absence from the forces
rationale: Both verses say God rejected the people and will not go out with their forces. Psalm43 adds their shame; Psalm59 introduces the statement with a question. The extended wording, including the army's lost divine accompaniment, is shared.

relationship: Defeat before enemies under divine action
rationale: The psalm attributes the people's retreat before enemies to God. Leviticus threatens falling before enemies and flight when God sets His face against the disobedient. The military reversal is comparable, but Psalm43:18 denies covenant unfaithfulness, so Leviticus's stated cause is not imposed on the lament.

relationship: Scattering among the nations
rationale: Psalm43 says God scattered the people among nations after handing them over like food sheep. Leviticus threatens scattering among the nations in its covenant sanctions. The scattering language corresponds, while the psalm's assertion of fidelity prevents treating the passages as identical explanations of guilt.

relationship: Becoming a parable among nations
rationale: The community says God made it a parable among nations. Deuteronomy's curses predict becoming a riddle, parable and tale among the nations. The particular description of public disgrace corresponds; the curse's disobedience setting is distinct from Psalm43's profession of covenant fidelity.

relationship: Shame covering the face
rationale: The psalm describes all-day humiliation and shame covering the speaker's face. Psalm68 joins endured reproach with embarrassment covering the face. Both express disgrace through that covering image, with Psalm68 explicitly saying the reproach was on God's account.

relationship: Affliction without forgetting divine instruction
rationale: Despite all that happened, the community says it did not forget God or act unjustly toward His covenant. Psalm118 says sinners' cords entangled the speaker but he did not forget God's law. Both set remembered fidelity against oppression, rather than assuming suffering proves apostasy.

relationship: Humiliation in death's shadow with different stated causes
rationale: Psalm43 says God humbled the people in affliction and covered them with death's shadow. Psalm106 describes people in death's shadow whose hearts were humbled in toil, then rescued. Psalm106 expressly attributes their plight to rejected divine counsel; Psalm43's surrounding profession of fidelity is preserved as a difference.

relationship: God awakening to act against enemies
rationale: Psalm43 asks why God sleeps and calls Him to awake and arise. Psalm77 narrates the Lord awakening like a sleeper and striking enemies backward. Both use waking for renewed divine action, while the lament's appeal is distinct from the later narration's simile.

relationship: Hidden face and apparent divine forgetting
rationale: Psalm43 asks why God turns His face away and forgets the people's poverty and affliction. Psalm12 combines the same two complaints, asking how long God will forget the speaker and turn His face away. The parallel keeps the communal and individual objects distinct.

relationship: The soul brought down to the ground
rationale: The community's soul is humbled to dust and its belly clings to earth. Psalm118 says the speaker's soul clung to the ground and asks for life. Both portray the soul's distress as prostration against the earth, with different accompanying petitions.

relationship: Help and rescue for God's name
rationale: Psalm43 asks God to arise, help and redeem for His name's sake. Psalm78 asks God the Savior to help and rescue for the glory of His name, also seeking propitiation for sins. The linked appeal to aid and the divine name is specific, without importing that confession into Psalm43.

relationship: The heading concerning those who will be changed
rationale: Both headings use the designation 'concerning those who will be changed.' Psalm44 also names the sons of Korah and a song of the beloved, whereas Psalm68 names David. The connection is the exact unusual heading, without assigning it an unexpressed musical meaning or common occasion.

relationship: The throne and upright scepter quoted concerning the Son
rationale: Hebrews expressly introduces the throne enduring for the age and the scepter of uprightness as words concerning the Son. These correspond to Psalm44's address to God concerning His enduring throne and upright royal rod.

relationship: Foreign gifts and royal homage
rationale: Psalm44 describes Tyre's daughters bowing to him with gifts and the rich entreating the addressed woman's favor. Psalm71 describes foreign kings offering gifts and bowing before the king. Both join foreign wealth and royal homage, without merging the different recipients or foreign groups.

relationship: Joyful entrance into royal or divine presence
rationale: The companions are led with gladness and exultation into the king's sanctuary. Psalm99 commands service to the Lord with gladness and entrance before Him with exultation. The paired expressions and movement into presence correspond, without identifying the psalm's royal procession as the same event.

relationship: An enduring royal name and the response of peoples
rationale: Psalm44 promises remembrance of the addressee's name through generations and the peoples' enduring thanksgiving. Psalm71 asks that the king's name remain blessed through the ages and describes all nations calling him blessed. Both connect the royal name's endurance with a response extending beyond one people.

relationship: God as refuge and help in distress
rationale: Psalm45 calls God refuge, strength and help in afflictions. Psalm9 says the Lord became refuge for the needy and helper at fitting times in distress. The paired descriptions of refuge and timely aid ground both statements of reliance.

relationship: Fearlessness grounded in God's presence
rationale: Psalm45's confession of God as refuge leads to refusal to fear even amid upheaval of earth and mountains. Psalm22 refuses fear even in death's shadow because God is with the speaker. The danger differs, but both expressly connect fearlessness in extreme peril with divine protection and presence.

relationship: The voices of waters before divine might
rationale: Psalm45 depicts waters roaring and mountains disturbed at His might. Psalm92 depicts rivers lifting their voices and calls both the sea's surges and the Lord on high wondrous. Both set the sounding waters alongside divine greatness, without making the two statements identical descriptions of what the mountains do.

relationship: A river associated with God's holy dwelling
rationale: Psalm45 joins a river's streams gladdening God's city with the Most High's sanctified dwelling. Ezekiel sees water flowing from the house by the altar and becoming a river that brings health and life. The holy dwelling and beneficial waters are comparable; the psalm does not identify its river as Ezekiel's vision.

relationship: Jerusalem's stability and God's presence
rationale: Psalm45 says God is in the city's midst, she will not be shaken and He will help her. Psalm124 says the one dwelling in Jerusalem will never be shaken and describes the Lord surrounding His people. Divine presence and protection explain the stated stability in both, with different spatial images.

relationship: The divine voice shaking the earth
rationale: Psalm45 describes God's voice and the earth being shaken amid disturbed nations and kingdoms. Psalm28 specifically attributes the shaking of the wilderness to the Lord's voice. Both assign the disturbance of a terrestrial place to divine speech.

relationship: Jacob's God as protector
rationale: The refrain confesses that Jacob's God is the community's supporter. Psalm19 asks that the name of Jacob's God protect the addressee in affliction. The particular designation and protective role connect assurance and petition.

relationship: Invitation to come and see God's works
rationale: Both verses invite the audience to come and see God's works. Psalm45 points to wonders on earth, while Psalm65 describes His counsels concerning humanity as fearsome. The repeated invitation frames divine deeds as grounds for recognition and praise.

relationship: God ending war by breaking weapons
rationale: Psalm45 describes God ending wars, shattering the bow, breaking a weapon and burning shields. Hosea promises that God will shatter bow, sword and war from the land. Both directly combine divine action against weapons with the cessation of war, without changing shields into chariots.

relationship: War ended through the removal of weapons
rationale: Psalm45 describes wars ended and weapons broken or burned. Isaiah describes nations beating swords into plows and spears into sickles and ceasing to wage war. Both connect peace with weapons losing their military use, while destruction and conversion into tools remain different actions.

relationship: Ceasing human action before God's power
rationale: Psalm45 commands the audience to cease activity and know God, following His ending of wars. Moses tells the people to stand and behold divine salvation, for the Lord will fight while they keep silence. Both place human cessation alongside recognition of divine action, without equating the two occasions.

relationship: Clapping and exultation in praise
rationale: Psalm46 calls all nations to clap their hands and shout to God with exultation. Psalm97 personifies rivers clapping and mountains exulting before divine judgment. The paired gestures of praise occur with human peoples and natural features as different subjects.

relationship: God as great King beyond one nation
rationale: Psalm46 calls the Most High a great King over all the earth. Malachi's divine rebuke declares, 'I am a great King,' and says His name is manifest among nations. The shared royal designation has a scope beyond one people, expressed in praise and rebuke respectively.

relationship: Peoples subjected beneath the speaker
rationale: Psalm46 says God subjected peoples under the community and nations under its feet. Psalm17 describes God subjecting peoples beneath the individual speaker. The action and spatial expression correspond, while the collective and individual recipients differ.

relationship: Divine choice, love and inheritance
rationale: Psalm46 says God chose His inheritance for the people, the beauty of Jacob whom He loved. Deuteronomy connects God's love of the fathers with choosing their seed and giving land to inherit. Both join choice, love and an inheritance given to the people, without changing 'His inheritance' into their independent choice.

relationship: Divine kingship over the nations
rationale: Psalm46 says God reigned over nations and sits on His holy throne. Psalm21 explains that kingship belongs to the Lord and He is master of the nations. Both explicitly connect divine kingship with authority over nations, not merely one earthly realm.

relationship: Weekday designations in Psalm headings
rationale: Psalm47's heading specifies the second day of the week, while Psalm23's specifies the first. The exact weekday notices form a concrete heading comparison; neither a shared author nor an unexpressed performance occasion is inferred.

relationship: The repeated acclamation of the Lord's greatness
rationale: Psalm47 declares the Lord great and greatly to be praised in His city and holy mountain. Psalm95 uses the same acclamation before calling Him fearsome above all gods. The repeated praise formula occurs with different following descriptions.

relationship: God's presence supporting the city
rationale: Psalm47 says God is known in her citadels when He supports her. Psalm45 says God is in the city's midst, preventing its shaking and bringing help. Both connect the city's security with divine presence and support, while keeping citadels and the city as distinct expressions.

relationship: A destructive wind and ships at sea
rationale: Psalm47 says a violent wind will shatter Tarshish ships. Ezekiel's address to the trading city describes the south wind shattering her in the sea after her rowers led her out. Wind-driven maritime destruction is comparable, but the wind, subject and occasion are not harmonized.

relationship: God founding Zion
rationale: Psalm47 says God founded His city forever after describing what was heard and seen there. Psalm86 names Mother Zion and says the Most High Himself founded her. Both expressly attribute the city's foundation to God, while Psalm86's verse does not repeat the temporal qualification.

relationship: God's name honored across the earth
rationale: Psalm47 extends God's praise, like His name, to the earth's limits. Malachi says His name has been glorified among nations from sunrise to sunset, with incense and pure sacrifice in every place. Both give the honor of God's name a worldwide scope, with different forms of worship specified.

relationship: Zion and Judea's daughters rejoicing at judgments
rationale: Both verses join Zion's rejoicing with the daughters of Judea exulting because of God's judgments. Psalm47 voices the desired response and Psalm96 describes it as heard and enacted; the distinctive combination is shared.

relationship: Telling the next generation
rationale: After commands concerning the city's strength and citadels, Psalm47 gives the purpose of telling another generation. Psalm77 repeatedly directs the transmission of God's deeds and instruction to children and the generation to come. The shared purpose is deliberate intergenerational testimony, with different material being described.

relationship: God shepherding His people
rationale: Psalm47 identifies the community's God forever and says He will shepherd them through the ages. Psalm22 confesses that the Lord shepherds the individual speaker. Both assign shepherding to God; the communal duration is not rewritten as shepherding only until death.

relationship: Rich and poor considered together
rationale: Psalm48 explicitly includes rich and poor together in its audience for teaching on wealth and mortality. Proverbs brings rich and poor together and says the Lord made both. The paired economic groups are jointly placed under a condition beyond their wealth, with mortality and common creation remaining different emphases.

relationship: Parables and riddles as modes of instruction
rationale: Psalm48 says the speaker will incline his ear to a parable and open a riddle with a psaltery. Psalm77 says he will open his mouth in parables and utter riddles from the beginning. The two named forms of enigmatic instruction correspond, without making listening and speaking the same action.

relationship: Wealth as an uncertain ground of confidence
rationale: Psalm48 introduces people boasting in wealth before discussing inability to pay redemption and the passing of possessions. Timothy is told to forbid the rich from arrogance and hope in uncertain wealth, directing hope to God. The connection concerns misplaced confidence, not a claim that every wealthy person has the same conduct.

relationship: The inability to purchase life
rationale: Psalm48 says a brother does not redeem, asks whether a person will redeem and says he will not give God his atonement price, continuing with the soul's redemption price in the next unit. Jesus asks what gain of the world benefits someone who forfeits life and what a person can give in exchange for life. Both question material means of securing life without resolving Psalm48:10's difficult syntax.

relationship: Wise and foolish dying while wealth passes to others
rationale: Psalm48 says foolish and senseless people perish and leave wealth to strangers after mentioning the wise dying. Ecclesiastes asks how the wise dies with the fool and laments leaving toil to a successor whose wisdom is unknown. Both join common mortality with loss of control over accumulated goods.

relationship: The grave or Hades described as a house
rationale: Psalm48 calls tombs the enduring houses of those who named lands after themselves. Job conditionally describes Hades as his house and gloom as his bedding. Both use domestic lodging for death's dwelling, while Job's personal lament is distinct from the psalm's observation about the wealthy.

relationship: Contrasting shepherds in the presence of death
rationale: Psalm48 pictures people as sheep placed in Hades with death shepherding them. Psalm22 names the Lord as shepherd and refuses fear while walking in death's shadow because He is present. The shepherd imagery and death setting create a precise contrast between the guides; no identical afterlife account is imposed.

relationship: Hope that God will not leave the soul to Hades
rationale: Psalm48 expects God to redeem the soul from Hades' hand when He receives the speaker. Psalm15 says God will not abandon the speaker's soul to Hades. Both place the soul's escape from Hades in God's action, with redemption and non-abandonment expressed differently.

relationship: Limits on carrying possessions beyond life
rationale: Psalm48 says the dying person will not take everything and his glory will not descend with him. Timothy states that people brought nothing into the world and cannot carry anything out. Both limit the retention of possessions beyond life; the psalm's 'not everything' is not silently changed into the letter's 'anything.'

relationship: Death pictured as enduring darkness
rationale: Psalm48 says the person will enter the generation of his fathers and never see light. Job anticipates going without return to a land of everlasting darkness with no brightness. Both portray departure into death as a lasting loss of light, without identifying the individual experiences.

relationship: The sunrise-to-sunset scope of divine address and praise
rationale: Psalm49 says God spoke and called the earth from the sun's risings to its settings. Psalm112 uses the same span to command praise of the Lord's name. The geographic or daily formula is shared, with divine summons and human praise remaining different actions.

relationship: Fire proceeding before God
rationale: Psalm49 describes fire burning before the coming God and a great tempest around Him. Psalm96 describes fire going ahead before Him and setting enemies aflame. Both give advancing fire a place in divine manifestation; the enemy-burning object belongs expressly to Psalm96.

relationship: Heaven and earth summoned for testimony concerning the people
rationale: Psalm49 calls heaven above and earth to the judging of God's people. Moses gathers the people's officers and calls heaven and earth as witnesses concerning them. The cosmic summons has a judicial setting in both, with God and Moses as different speakers.

relationship: Covenant made over sacrifices
rationale: Psalm49 calls for God's holy ones who made His covenant over sacrifices to be gathered. Exodus narrates burnt offerings and calves, the reading of the covenant book, and covenant blood sprinkled on the people. It supplies a concrete covenant-and-sacrifice comparison without claiming the psalm's gathering is the same ceremony.

relationship: Heavens declaring God's righteousness
rationale: Psalm49 says the heavens will announce His righteousness because God is judge. Psalm96 says the heavens announced His righteousness and all peoples saw His glory. The distinctive heavenly proclamation is shared, with future and completed forms preserved.

relationship: God's covenant self-identification to Israel
rationale: God addresses Israel with 'I am God, your God' while announcing testimony against it. The commandments open with the Lord identifying Himself as Israel's God who brought it from Egypt. The repeated self-identification frames divine address to the same covenant people without adding the exodus clause to the psalm.

relationship: The world and its fullness belong to God
rationale: Psalm49 explains that God would not tell humans if hungry because the inhabited world and its fullness are His. Psalm23 declares that the earth, its fullness, the inhabited world and its inhabitants belong to the Lord. The ownership statement is the particular basis shared by the two passages.

relationship: Calling in distress, rescue and grateful acknowledgment
rationale: God invites a call in affliction, promises rescue and says the rescued person will glorify Him. Psalm106 recounts people crying in affliction and being rescued, then calls them to acknowledge God's mercies and wonders. The sequence links appeal, divine rescue and the human response of praise.

relationship: Religious instruction contradicted by conduct
rationale: God asks a sinner why he recites divine decrees and carries the covenant in his mouth; the following accusations include theft and adultery. Romans challenges the person instructed in law who teaches against stealing and adultery yet transgresses. The comparison is the specific mismatch between professed instruction and conduct, not an accusation against every member of a people.

relationship: Casting God's words behind the body
rationale: The psalm accuses the sinner of hating instruction and casting God's words behind him. Nehemiah's confession says the people cast God's law behind their bodies while withdrawing from Him. The unusual bodily image expresses deliberate rejection of divine instruction in both.

relationship: Evil and deceitful speech
rationale: Psalm49 accuses the mouth of multiplying wickedness and the tongue of weaving deceit. Psalm33 commands restraint of the tongue from evil and lips from deceit. The paired evils and organs of speech correspond in accusation and admonition.

relationship: Hostility involving brothers and a mother's sons
rationale: Psalm49 describes speech against one's brother and a stumbling block against one's mother's son. Psalm68 describes the speaker estranged from brothers and a foreigner to his mother's sons. Both use the paired kinship expressions for fractured family relations, without equating slander with estrangement or identifying the speakers.

relationship: Divine forbearance followed by exposure of wrongdoing
rationale: Psalm49 says God's silence was mistaken for likeness to the sinner, before He promises rebuke and exposure. Isaiah says God sees and overlooks the addressee, who did not fear Him, then promises to proclaim His righteousness and the person's evils. Both join withheld immediate response with disregard and coming disclosure, using different descriptions of that response.

relationship: same-chapter return to the praising sacrifice
rationale: The closing verse says a praising sacrifice glorifies God and connects the way with divine salvation. It returns to the command to offer a praising sacrifice in verse14, enclosing the intervening rebuke with the poem's positive account of worship.

relationship: God wiping out lawless acts
rationale: Psalm50 appeals to divine mercy and compassion for the blotting out of lawless acts. Isaiah presents God as the One who wipes out lawless acts and will not remember. The erasure of wrongdoing corresponds as requested mercy and divine declaration.

relationship: Hyssop and sprinkling for cleansing
rationale: Psalm50 anticipates sprinkling with hyssop and becoming clean. Leviticus includes hyssop in the rite whose sprinkling declares a person cleansed from leprosy. The distinctive material and cleansing action correspond, without asserting that the penitent's sin is a diagnosis of leprosy.

relationship: Joy and bones expressing praise
rationale: Psalm50 anticipates hearing exultation and joy so that humbled bones will exult. Psalm34 anticipates the soul's exultation and all the bones saying that no one is like the rescuing Lord. Both give the bones a voice or action within restored joy, with distinct statements about what the bones do.

relationship: Cleansing, a new heart and renewed spirit
rationale: The psalm asks God to create a clean heart and renew an upright spirit within the speaker. Ezekiel promises cleansing, a new heart and new spirit, followed by God's own Spirit placed within the people. Both locate inward renewal in divine action, while the psalm's upright spirit is not simply equated with every spirit expression in Ezekiel.

relationship: The feared removal of God's Spirit
rationale: Psalm50 asks God not to remove His holy Spirit from the speaker. Samuel describes the Lord's Spirit departing from Saul. The narrative gives a specific contrast to the prayer against removal; it does not identify Saul as this psalm's speaker.

relationship: Joy in divine salvation
rationale: Psalm50 asks restoration of the exultation of God's salvation. Psalm12 anticipates the heart exulting in God's salvation after hope in mercy. The particular joy is tied to salvation in both; the request for restoration and the anticipated response remain distinct.

relationship: Teaching God's way to those needing correction
rationale: Psalm50 anticipates teaching God's ways to the lawless so the ungodly turn back to Him. Psalm24 says the Lord gives sinners instruction in the way and teaches the meek His ways. Both connect divine ways and instruction directed toward those needing guidance, with the penitent and God as different teachers.

relationship: Bloodshed in the Nathan and David context
rationale: Psalm50 asks rescue from bloodshed, and its heading names Nathan's visit after Bathsheba. In that visit Nathan specifically accuses David of killing Uriah through the sons of Ammon. The narrative supplies concrete bloodshed within the named context; the psalm's request itself does not name Uriah or specify the exact sense of deliverance.

relationship: Sacrifices and burnt offerings not desired
rationale: Psalm50 says a desired sacrifice would have been given, but God will not delight in burnt offerings. Psalm39 says God did not desire sacrifice and offering or request burnt and sin offerings. The explicit negative statements concerning these offerings correspond; Psalm50's later restored offerings are still read in context.

relationship: God's favorable regard for the brokenhearted
rationale: Psalm50 calls a broken spirit God's sacrifice and says He will not despise a broken and humbled heart. Isaiah describes the Most High giving patience to the fainthearted and life to the brokenhearted. Both affirm divine regard for brokenhearted people, without changing Isaiah's resting among holy ones into a different dwelling claim.

relationship: Jerusalem's wall and God's favorable action
rationale: The psalm asks God to do good to Zion and build Jerusalem's walls. Nehemiah calls for rebuilding Jerusalem's wall and reports God's good hand upon him. The particular city, wall-building and favorable divine action correspond, without assigning the psalm's request to Nehemiah's historical occasion.

relationship: A sacrifice of righteousness
rationale: Psalm50 anticipates God's delight in a sacrifice of righteousness after the prayer for Zion and Jerusalem. Psalm4 commands offering a sacrifice of righteousness and hoping in the Lord. The specific description of acceptable sacrifice connects the passages and qualifies any reading of Psalm50 as rejecting every offering without distinction.
